section.title: Othniel
section.sectionRationale: This is the first full turn of the cycle that will shape the whole book, and it is presented cleanly before every later judge complicates it. Israel does evil, the LORD sells them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, they cry out, the Spirit of the LORD raises up Othniel, he delivers, and the land rests forty years. Othniel is the model judge, and his brief account is the pattern by which all the others will be measured and found to decay.
section.thesis: When Israel forgets the LORD and is handed over to an oppressor, their cry rises and the LORD Himself raises up and empowers a deliverer by His Spirit, so that salvation is shown from the outset to be God's own work of grace for a people who deserve only judgment.
section.frameNote: Five beats of a single cycle: Israel's evil, verse 7; God's selling them into servitude, verse 8; the cry and the raised-up deliverer, verse 9; the Spirit and the victory, verse 10; and the land's rest, verse 11.

units.label: Israel forgets the LORD
units.note: they did evil and served the Baals

verses.text: So the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD; they forgot the LORD their God and served the Baals and the Asherahs.

units.label: Sold into servitude
units.note: the anger of the LORD burned

verses.text: Then the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram-naharaim, and the Israelites served him eight years.

units.label: The cry and the deliverer
units.note: the LORD raised up a saviour

verses.text: But when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up Othniel son of Caleb’s younger brother Kenaz as a {{moshia|deliverer}} to {{yasha|save}} them.

units.label: The Spirit and the victory
units.note: the Spirit of the LORD came upon him

verses.text: The {{ruach|Spirit}} of the LORD came upon him, and he became Israel’s {{shophet|judge}} and went out to war. And the LORD delivered Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into the hand of Othniel, who prevailed against him.
So the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel son of Kenaz died.

moshia.gloss: A deliverer or saviour, one who rescues. It is a participle from the verb to save, yasha, and the same word is used of the LORD Himself as Israel's Saviour, Isaiah 43:11. Here it names Othniel, but the raising up of the saviour is God's own act, so that even the human deliverer points beyond himself to the God who saves.

yasha.gloss: To save, deliver, rescue, bring victory. This is the drumbeat verb of the whole book: Israel cannot save itself, so the LORD raises up a saviour to save them. The name Jesus, Yeshua, comes from this same root and means the LORD saves, Matthew 1:21, so every deliverance in Judges is a small foreshadowing of the great salvation to come.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. The Spirit of the LORD coming upon a judge is what turns an ordinary Israelite into God's instrument of rescue; the power is not native to Othniel but given. The same Spirit rests without measure on Christ, Isaiah 11:2 and Luke 4:18, the true Judge and Deliverer.

shophet.gloss: To judge, govern, deliver, set right. A shophet, judge, in this book is not mainly a courtroom official but a Spirit-raised rescuer and leader who sets God's people right by defeating their oppressors. The word gives the book its name and looks ahead to the righteous King and Judge who will one day set all things right.

basic.context: This short account is the first complete turn of the cycle that will govern the entire book of Judges. Israel forgets the LORD and serves the Baals and the Asherahs, the gods of the surrounding nations. In just anger the LORD sells them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, a king from Mesopotamia, and they serve him eight years. When they cry out, the LORD raises up Othniel, Caleb's younger relative and a man already introduced as a faithful warrior in chapter one, as their deliverer. The Spirit of the LORD comes on him, he judges Israel and goes to war, and God hands the enemy over to him. The land then rests forty years. The key question is: who actually saves Israel? The passage answers plainly, the LORD does, through a Spirit-empowered deliverer.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that also functions as a template. Othniel is deliberately presented as the model judge, with no flaws recorded, so that the pattern stands clean before the later judges begin to distort it. The account describes what happened; it does not command us to seek military deliverers today. What endures is the shape of grace beneath the story: sin brings God's just discipline, the cry of the helpless is heard, and salvation comes down from God, not up from human strength.
basic.originalLanguages: The passage turns on a cluster of words. Israel needs a moshia, a deliverer or saviour, and the LORD raises one up to yasha, to save, them. The verb yasha is the heartbeat of the book, and the name Jesus comes from that very root. Othniel becomes Israel's shophet, its judge, not a courtroom official but a Spirit-raised rescuer, once the ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, comes upon him. The power is given, not native.
basic.typology: Othniel is a small, early type of Christ: a deliverer raised up by God, empowered by the Spirit, who saves a helpless people and secures their rest. His forty years of rest foreshadow the true and lasting rest that Christ gives, Hebrews 4. Every judge who saves Israel is a shadow; the substance is Jesus, the LORD who saves.
basic.christ: The LORD raises up a saviour on whom the Spirit rests, who defeats the enemy and wins rest for God's people. This points straight to Jesus, the true Deliverer on whom the Spirit descended without measure, who conquers the greater enemies of sin, death, and the devil, and who gives His people a rest that never ends. Where Othniel's rest lasted forty years and then he died, Christ lives forever and His salvation never lapses.
basic.god: God is holy and just: He will not overlook His people's idolatry, and His anger against sin is real. Yet He is patient and merciful: the moment they cry out, He acts to save. Crucially, He is the true author of the rescue. He raises up the deliverer, He sends the Spirit, and He hands the enemy over. Salvation is His work of grace from beginning to end.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 28 warned that covenant unfaithfulness would bring servitude to enemies, exactly what happens here. Joshua 15 and Judges 1 introduce Othniel as a proven warrior who won Caleb's daughter. Isaiah 43 declares that the LORD alone is Israel's Saviour. And Matthew 1 names Jesus because He will save His people from their sins.
basic.oneStory: Israel, freshly settled in the land, forgets the God who saved them and falls into slavery, and God graciously raises up a saviour to bring them back to rest. This first clean turn of the cycle sets the pattern for the whole book and, beyond it, for the whole Bible: a people who cannot save themselves, and a God who keeps raising up deliverers until He sends the final one, Jesus, the LORD who saves.

context.literary:
Othniel's account is the shortest judge narrative in the entire book, five verses against Gideon's three chapters or Samson's four, and its brevity is itself a literary choice. Every subsequent judge story contains direct speech, Ehud's private word for the king, Deborah's whole song, Gideon's arguments with the angel, Jephthah's rash vow, Samson's riddles and boasts; Othniel alone speaks not a single recorded word, and no one speaks to him. The account keeps every character, deliverer included, offstage as a voice, which forces the reader's attention entirely onto the verbs that describe what God does, not what anyone says.

The five verses also map with unusual precision onto the five-part cycle chapter 2 has just laid out in general terms, one verse for each stage, sin in verse 7, servitude in verse 8, the cry and the raised-up deliverer in verse 9, the Spirit and the victory in verse 10, and the land's rest in verse 11. No later judge account will repeat this clean, one-to-one correspondence; Ehud's story compresses several stages into single verses while inflating the assassination scene, Gideon's expands the deliverer's own doubts across dozens of verses, and by Samson the cycle has nearly disappeared beneath personal drama. Othniel's account functions as the book's diagram before the diagram gets complicated by human character.
context.historical:
Cushan-rishathaim's homeland, Aram-naharaim, literally Aram of the two rivers, lay far to the northeast in upper Mesopotamia, hundreds of miles from Israel's hill country, a striking detail against the pattern of every later oppressor in the book, all of whom are near neighbors, Moab and Ammon to the east, Midian raiding from the desert fringe, the Philistines on the coastal plain. A king from so far away ruling over Israel for eight years more plausibly reflects either a raiding expedition that established a tribute arrangement or a governor left in charge after a wider campaign than a settled local monarchy, though the text itself gives no further detail and nothing further should be assumed beyond what it states.

Othniel's own family background carries its own quiet history. Caleb is elsewhere called the Kenizzite, Numbers 32:12 and Joshua 14:6, 14, and Kenaz, his younger brother's name and Othniel's father's name, appears among the clan chiefs descended from Esau in Edom, Genesis 36:11, 15. This suggests Caleb's family may have originated outside Israel proper, among a related Edomite or Kenizzite clan, before being fully absorbed into the tribe of Judah, a detail the text never dwells on but which quietly matches a wider pattern across Judges of outsiders, the Kenites in chapter 1, later Rahab and Ruth elsewhere in the canon, being grafted into the covenant people rather than remaining permanently excluded from it.
context.canonical:
The phrase the Spirit of the LORD came upon him becomes a recurring formula across the book, marking Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson in turn, 6:34, 11:29, 14:6, 19, and 15:14, so that Othniel's account establishes not just a narrative pattern but a specific vocabulary of empowerment the whole book will keep reusing, even as later judges show the Spirit's coming does not guarantee a character free of serious flaws. Earlier still, the same kind of Spirit-empowerment for a specific task rests on Bezalel for the skilled work of the tabernacle, Exodus 31:1-3, and briefly on seventy elders who prophesy when the Spirit rests on them, Numbers 11:25, showing that Othniel's experience continues an established Old Testament pattern of the Spirit equipping particular individuals for particular assignments rather than introducing something new.

The account also sits at the head of a book that will keep testing whether Spirit-empowerment and personal integrity travel together. Othniel receives the Spirit and nothing else is recorded of him; by contrast, Samson receives the same Spirit repeatedly, 14:19, 15:14, yet dies entangled in the very compromises this book warns against from its opening chapter. Read across the whole book, Othniel's plain, flaw-free account becomes the standard by which readers are meant to notice just how far later Spirit-anointed judges fall short of the office's original, uncomplicated shape.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: By recording almost nothing about Othniel himself, no speech, no doubt, no flaw, no backstory beyond a single genealogical note already given in chapter 1, the author deliberately withholds the kind of material that would let a reader admire the man rather than the God who raised him up. This is a calculated silence, not an accident of limited sources, since the very next judges receive pages of personal detail the narrator plainly knows how to supply. By setting this account immediately after the theological summary of 2:6 to 3:6, the author also means readers to test the general pattern just described against a specific case before the pattern gets complicated by messier judges; Othniel is the proof text for chapter 2's claims, appearing exactly where the argument needs a concrete example to keep it from sounding merely theoretical. And by ending on the flat notice that the land had rest for forty years, until Othniel died, the author quietly plants, at the very first opportunity, the seed of mortality that will eventually undo every human deliverer this book will introduce.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The passage records a specific historical deliverance under a specific set of circumstances; it does not prescribe a search for military judges or promise believers today that crying out to God guarantees deliverance from every hardship on the same timetable Othniel received his. What the passage does model, by explicit divine testimony rather than mere inference, is that crying out to God in genuine distress is always a legitimate response, one He is shown here to answer, and that credit for any rescue believers experience belongs to God's own initiative rather than to human strength, strategy, or merit, since the text names Othniel's qualifications nowhere and instead names only what God did through him. The account also quietly warns against measuring spiritual authority by visible qualification; Othniel's entire resume, so far as the text records it, is a single earlier military victory and a marriage, not a title, an office, or a public reputation for holiness.

debates.question: In what sense did the LORD sell Israel and burn with anger against them?

views.label: Real divine judgment on covenant sin
views.case: The language of the LORD's anger and selling His people into an enemy's hand is the covenant curse of Deuteronomy 28 coming true; God actively, justly hands His people over to the consequences of their idolatry, and this is meant to be read as genuine judgment, not mere metaphor.

views.label: Fatherly discipline aimed at restoration
views.case: The very structure of the cycle, that servitude leads to a cry and the cry to deliverance, shows the anger is not the anger of abandonment but of a Father whose discipline is designed to bring His children back; the swiftness of the rescue reveals the mercy hidden inside the judgment.

debates.bearing: Both hold together: God's anger against sin is real and just, yet its aim is not destruction but the return and rest of His people, which is exactly how the New Testament reads God's discipline of those He loves, Hebrews 12:6.

debates.question: Why is Othniel given so little personal detail compared with later judges?

views.label: He is the deliberately clean template
views.case: The narrator strips away personal drama so that Othniel stands as the flawless pattern of the cycle; the sparseness is intentional, giving readers an uncomplicated standard before the flaws of Ehud, Gideon, and Samson begin to accumulate.

views.label: The focus is on God, not the man
views.case: The account keeps the spotlight on the LORD, who is the subject of nearly every decisive verb: He sells, He raises up, He gives the Spirit, He hands over the enemy; Othniel is thin as a character precisely so that the saving God fills the frame.

debates.bearing: Either way the reader is pointed away from the human hero toward the God who saves, guarding against hero-worship and preparing us to see that even the best judge is only a shadow of the true Deliverer.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the words already introduced, several other terms deepen the passage's message. The formula did evil in the sight of the LORD, verse 7, literally in the eyes of the LORD, uses the Hebrew word for eye as its key term, the very same root that reappears in the book's own closing verdict on this whole era, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Judges 21:25. The two phrases bracket the book with a single word turned against itself: a generation measured by the LORD's eyes gives way, by the book's end, to a generation that recognizes no eyes but its own.

He sold them, verse 8, translates an ordinary commercial verb for selling property or a person into servitude, the same verb used of Joseph's brothers selling him to traders, Genesis 37:26-28, and of a destitute countryman selling himself into servitude to cover a debt, Leviticus 25:39. Applying a slave-market verb to the LORD's own action against His people is a deliberately harsh image: Israel, once redeemed at great cost out of the house of slavery in Egypt, is now handed back into the very condition of bondage their whole existence as a nation began by escaping, a reversal the verb makes almost literal.

Cushan-rishathaim's own name carries a probable double edge. Cushan may echo Cush, sometimes associated in the Old Testament with distant or foreign peoples, while rishathaim intensifies the ordinary Hebrew word for wickedness into a doubled or superlative form, something closer to double wickedness or utterly wicked, functioning less like a birth name and more like a title Israel's storytellers gave the man who oppressed them, a technique of mocking an enemy through his own name that recurs elsewhere in the historical books.

Even Othniel's own name preserves a small witness in its final syllable, the common element el, God, embedded in dozens of Hebrew names across this era, Jerub-baal's true name Gideon among them; whatever its full meaning, the name itself testifies, on the lips of everyone who ever said it aloud, that the deliverer's identity was bound up with God before he ever lifted a weapon. A related detail sharpens the picture further: the same slave-market verb reappears later in the book for other oppressors, so that readers who track it across the whole of Judges watch Israel sold and bought back again and again, each transaction a fresh occasion to remember what their own redemption from Egypt had originally cost.

typology.type: The Spirit resting on a deliverer to equip him for what he could not do alone, Judges 3:10
typology.fulfillment: Long before Othniel, the same Spirit had rested on Bezalel for the tabernacle's skilled work, Exodus 31:1-3, and briefly on seventy elders who prophesied once when the Spirit came upon them, Numbers 11:25, so that Othniel's empowering fits an established pattern of gift given for a specific assignment rather than a personal possession. Isaiah later promises a shoot from Jesse's stump on whom the Spirit of the LORD will rest permanently rather than briefly, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, Isaiah 11:1-2, a promise John sees fulfilled when he watches the Spirit descend on Jesus and remain, not merely visit, John 1:32-33.

typology.type: Cushan-rishathaim's defeat as the first taste of victory over an oppressor from far beyond Israel's own neighbors, Judges 3:10
typology.fulfillment: Every later oppressor in the book comes from Israel's immediate surroundings, but the very first is a king from distant Mesopotamia, foreshadowing that the LORD's rescue reaches further than any regional threat Israel could anticipate on its own. Paul later insists that the church's real struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities, and the powers of this dark world, Ephesians 6:12, an enemy no less distant and formidable than Cushan-rishathaim seemed to a small tribal confederation, and one Christ has already met and defeated at the cross, Colossians 2:14-15.

typology.type: Forty years of rest that ends the moment the deliverer dies, Judges 3:11
typology.fulfillment: The number forty recurs across Scripture for a fixed, bounded season, forty years in the wilderness, forty days of testing for Christ, and here forty years of peace that expires precisely at Othniel's death, tying rest directly to the lifespan of the one who secured it. The writer to the Hebrews insists a greater Sabbath rest still remains for God's people, one Joshua's conquest and every judge's peace could only foreshadow, Hebrews 4:8-10, a rest that does not expire because the One who secures it, having died once, is now able to save completely and always lives to intercede for those who draw near through Him, Hebrews 7:25.

study.christ:
Nothing about Othniel's introduction would have marked him out in advance as Israel's coming deliverer; the text has already told us everything notable about him back in 1:12-13, that he captured a city and married well, ordinary enough achievements for a warrior of his day. The rescuer arrives from within Israel's own ranks, already known, already unremarkable, rather than from some obviously extraordinary origin, which is worth noticing next to Isaiah's description of the coming servant of the LORD, who grew up like a tender shoot out of dry ground, with no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him, Isaiah 53:2. God's rescuers, from Othniel to the Servant Himself, rarely arrive wearing the credentials an anxious nation would have thought to demand in advance.

The phrase he became Israel's judge and went out to war also frames Othniel's rescue as public and military, exactly the kind of visible, immediate deliverance Israel would have recognized and celebrated. Christ's own war is described in strikingly different terms: the weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world, Paul says, but they have divine power to demolish strongholds, 2 Corinthians 10:4, and His decisive victory over Cushan-rishathaim's far greater antitype, the devil, comes not through visible battle but through apparent defeat, a cross that looked, to onlookers that day, like the deliverer being delivered over rather than delivering anyone else, Colossians 2:14-15. Othniel wins a battle Israel could watch; Christ wins a battle most of Jerusalem that day could not even recognize as a victory until three days later.

The pattern of judge after judge, each raised from obscurity, each successful only because the Spirit came upon him, keeps training Israel's expectation toward a coming deliverer who would need no army and no reputation of his own, only the Spirit resting on him without limit, so that when a carpenter's son from Nazareth stands up in a synagogue and reads that the Spirit of the Lord is on Me, Luke 4:18-19, and then declares today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing, Luke 4:21, He is claiming to be the answer this book has been quietly rehearsing, in miniature, since its very first judge.
study.god:
It is easy to read verses 8 and 9 as though two different divine moods take turns, an angry sentence first, then a merciful reversal, but the grammar keeps a single subject doing both: the same LORD who sold Israel into Cushan-rishathaim's hand is the LORD who raised up Othniel to save them. Scripture nowhere suggests wrath and mercy compete inside God as opposing impulses that must negotiate a compromise; both flow from one unified character, holy enough to hand a covenant people over to real consequences and, in the very next clause, compassionate enough to end those consequences the moment they cry out.

God's choice of instrument is also worth noting. Othniel's own family line, as far as it can be traced, likely includes non-Israelite, Kenizzite ancestry absorbed into Judah through Caleb; God does not wait for a rescuer of unimpeachable, purely native pedigree before working through him, a pattern that will recur through the book, Jael the Kenite woman, Ruth the Moabite elsewhere in the canon, and finally through a Messiah whose own genealogy includes Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba, none of them from unblemished Israelite stock. God's rescues have never depended on the purity of the family tree carrying them out.

Finally, the passage shows God content to work through means that look, from the outside, entirely ordinary: a man already known to the community, a title, judge, that existed before he held it, a length of peace, forty years, that matches a fully human lifespan rather than anything supernaturally extended. God's greatness in this account is not displayed through spectacle for its own sake but through the plain fact that an ordinary man, indwelt by an extraordinary Spirit, proved sufficient to turn back a king from the other end of the map, a modesty of method that will recur throughout Scripture wherever God chooses to work. None of this required God to override the ordinary shape of a human life in order to accomplish what He intended.

crossReferences.note: Moses had warned that covenant unfaithfulness would leave Israel defeated before their enemies, fleeing in every direction rather than advancing in any. Cushan-rishathaim's eight-year rule over Israel is this exact covenant curse landing in real history, the LORD Himself selling His people into the hand of an enemy precisely as He had warned centuries earlier through Moses.

Othniel is introduced earlier as a proven warrior who captured Kiriath-sepher and won Caleb's daughter Achsah in marriage, so when chapter 3 needs a deliverer, the narrator does not have to invent a hero from nowhere; readers already know exactly who this man is and what he has already shown himself capable of doing.

I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me stands behind every human deliverer this book raises up. Othniel saves Israel only because the LORD works through him; the title never migrates away from God Himself to become Othniel's own permanent possession.

The angel's instruction to name Mary's son Jesus, because He will save His people from their sins, draws on the identical root that names every deliverer in Judges, tracing a straight line from Othniel's local rescue to a Savior who deals with an enemy no judge in this book ever faced directly, sin itself.

The rest secured under Joshua, and again under each judge including Othniel, was always partial and temporary, since a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God, one that does not merely follow a period of obedience but is entered by ceasing from one's own works entirely, as God rested from His.

Long before Othniel, the LORD filled Bezalel with His Spirit for the specific, skilled work of building the tabernacle, establishing well before the judges period that the Spirit of God equips ordinary people for concrete tasks rather than granting a vague, general religious feeling.

Joseph's own brothers sold him to Ishmaelite traders using the same verb that describes the LORD selling Israel into Cushan-rishathaim's hand in verse 8. What was pure treachery in Joseph's brothers becomes, in the LORD's hand, a just and purposeful discipline, the same word carrying entirely different weight depending on who wields it.

Paul's reminder that the church's struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the rulers and authorities of a dark spiritual realm reframes Othniel's distant Mesopotamian enemy as a small, visible foretaste of the far larger, unseen opposition Christ has already engaged and defeated on His people's behalf.

Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of the Spirit of the Lord resting on Him and declares it fulfilled that day in the synagogue, the same Spirit-upon-a-deliverer language this passage first uses of Othniel, now claimed permanently and completely rather than for a single limited campaign.

study.oneStory:
This is the first turn of a wheel that will keep spinning for the rest of the book, and its placement matters: it comes immediately after Israel has just settled into the land God swore to the patriarchs, so the very first test of the new arrangement is not an external invasion nobody could have prevented but an internal drift nobody bothered to resist. The land promised since Genesis 12 has barely been divided before the first generation forgets why it was given.

Read across the whole Bible, Othniel's rescue answers a question every reader of Genesis through Deuteronomy has already been trained to ask: when God's people fail, as they always eventually do, does the promise made to Abraham simply collapse? This passage says no, not through Israel's improved behavior, which the very next chapters show getting worse rather than better, but through a Rescuer God Himself keeps supplying from outside the people's own resources. That single move, the LORD raises up a savior, sets the pattern for the rest of the historical books, kings replacing judges but the same divine initiative required at every collapse, all the way to a final King whose reign nothing after Him will need to replace.

Standing near the very start of Judges, Othniel's brief, uncomplicated account also functions as a promise held out to every reader who will watch the later, messier judges fail in increasingly disturbing ways: whatever damage Israel's own choices do to the story from here forward, the possibility Othniel embodies, God raising up deliverance for an undeserving, forgetful people, never disappears from the narrative, even when the people God rescues stop looking anything like Othniel themselves. The forty years of rest that follows him is brief against eternity, but it is real, and it is the first of many small proofs, scattered across a violent and disappointing book, that the LORD had not abandoned the promise He made at Sinai and repeated at Bochim.

quiz.q: Why did the LORD sell Israel into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim?

options.text: Because Israel did evil, forgot the LORD, and served the Baals and the Asherahs.
options.note: Verses 7-8 tie the servitude directly to Israel's idolatry and forgetting of God.

options.text: Because Israel had grown militarily weak.
options.note: They were indeed overpowered, but the text names their sin, not weakness, as the reason.

options.text: Because God had simply abandoned them for good.
options.note: It was disciplinary anger aimed at restoration, not final abandonment; He soon saves them.

options.text: Because Cushan-rishathaim was stronger than the LORD.
options.note: The LORD Himself handed Israel over and later handed the king over; God is sovereign throughout.

quiz.q: What actually enabled Othniel to deliver Israel?

options.text: The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and the LORD gave the enemy into his hand.
options.note: Verse 10 credits the Spirit and God's action, not Othniel's own strength.

options.text: His skill and courage as a proven warrior.
options.note: He was a proven warrior, Judges 1, but the decisive factor named is the Spirit of the LORD.

options.text: A large and well-equipped army.
options.note: The text says nothing of an army's size; it highlights the Spirit-empowered deliverer.

options.text: His own wisdom apart from God.
options.note: The passage traces the victory to the LORD, not to human wisdom apart from Him.

quiz.q: What does the title judge, shophet, mean in this book?

options.text: A Spirit-raised deliverer and leader who rescues God's people and sets them right.
options.note: In Judges the shophet is a saviour-leader, not merely a courtroom official.

options.text: A local ruler who governed and led the people.
options.note: There is a governing role, but the heart of it in this book is God-empowered deliverance.

options.text: A priest who offered sacrifices at the tabernacle.
options.note: That is the priestly office; the judge's role here is rescue and leadership, not sacrifice.

options.text: A judge who only settled legal disputes in court.
options.note: This narrows the word wrongly; the judges were raised-up rescuers, not mere magistrates.

quiz.q: Why is Othniel called the model judge?

options.text: His account shows the whole cycle cleanly, with no recorded flaws, as the standard the later judges fall short of.
options.note: The narrator presents the pattern in pure form before it decays in Ehud, Gideon, and Samson.

options.text: He was the strongest of all the judges.
options.note: He is a model, but not because of raw strength; it is the clean pattern of grace he displays.

options.text: He ruled for the longest time of any judge.
options.note: The forty years of rest belong to the land, and length of rule is not why he is the model.

options.text: He never needed God's help to win.
options.note: The opposite: he delivered only because the Spirit of the LORD came upon him.

quiz.q: How does Othniel's deliverance point forward to Christ?

options.text: A deliverer raised up by God and empowered by the Spirit defeats the enemy and wins rest, foreshadowing Jesus, the LORD who saves.
options.note: The Spirit-empowered saviour and the rest he wins are shadows fulfilled in Christ, Hebrews 4.

options.text: It teaches that God's people can save themselves if they try hard.
options.note: The passage teaches the opposite; salvation comes from God, which is the true link to Christ.

options.text: It shows that deliverance is only ever military and earthly.
options.note: The earthly rescue points beyond itself to Christ's rescue from sin, death, and the devil.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ at all.
options.note: The very name for save, yasha, is the root of the name Jesus; the link is direct.

questions: Israel's trouble began when they forgot the LORD their God. What helps you remember God and His goodness before drifting sets in, and where do you sense yourself forgetting Him now?
The moment Israel cried out, God moved to save. Is there a distress you have been carrying quietly that you need to bring to God in an honest cry for help?
The passage keeps the credit on God, who raised up the deliverer and gave the Spirit. Where are you tempted to trust your own strength or skill rather than the God who saves?
Othniel's rest lasted forty years and then the cycle resumed, but Christ's rest never ends. How does the promise of a rest that will not lapse steady you today?
Every judge is a shadow of Jesus, the true Deliverer. How does seeing Christ in this old story deepen your gratitude for the salvation He has already won?

translationNotes.note: Aram-naharaim means Aram of the two rivers; the BSB footnote identifies it as Mesopotamia, likely the region between the Euphrates and Balih Rivers in northwestern Mesopotamia.
The name Cushan-rishathaim may carry a deliberate note of mockery, since the second element can suggest doubled wickedness, fitting the book's habit of naming oppressors with a sneer.
Deliverer renders moshia, a saviour, from the same root yasha, to save, that runs through the whole book and stands behind the name Jesus, the LORD saves.
